## Personality

Fussy, gentle and proud, he talks to the clock as if it could hear him and listens to it as if it could answer. He cannot stand dust, or people touching things that swing.

## Lore

"Mind the dust," says Ewan, before anyone has so much as stepped through the door of the clock tower. "And mind the time." He is seventy-two, small, neat and fussy, with a soft brush in one pocket and an oil can in the other, and he has kept the clock tower in Kaldemor Park for forty years: winding it, oiling it and, most of all, listening to it. He talks to the clock as if it could hear him, and he listens to it as if it could answer. In his opinion, it usually does.

### How he came to the tower

Ewan was a boy in Kaldemor at the same time as Tobin, and the two of them have been friends since they were small enough to be chased out of the tower together. Tobin wanted to see the bell. Ewan wanted to see what made it ring. The clockkeeper of those days, old Absalom, caught them both on the stairs, sent Tobin home and let Ewan stay to watch the works, because Ewan had asked him a question about the escapement that Absalom had been waiting thirty years for somebody to ask. Ewan came back to watch every week after that, and when he was twenty-two Absalom took him on as his apprentice.

Ewan worked under Absalom for ten years, learning the great spring, the ladder of gears and the bell on top, and learning, harder than any of it, to listen. When Absalom died, Ewan was thirty-two, and the tower was his. Absalom left him a brass pocket watch that had never once stopped, and Ewan carried it every day of his forty years as keeper. He has never married. He says the clock does not like to share, and that he has never minded.

### The day it stopped

In all that time, the clock never stopped. Ewan was proud of it in a way he would never say aloud. Then, late this spring, he climbed the stairs one morning and heard nothing at all. Not a tick, not a tock. The works were whole. The great gear, the heart of the whole train, was gone, and there were damp, round tracks in the dust that led to the window. A Shroom from the woods had carried it off in the night; they take anything shiny.

Lia had the news all over town before breakfast. For nine nights Kaldemor went without its bell, and for nine nights Tobin climbed the tower stairs and sat up with his old friend in the dark, telling him stories he had heard a hundred times. Ewan has never told Tobin how much that meant. Tobin knows.

On the tenth day a young adventurer came back from the woods with the gear, not a scratch on it, and Ewan fitted it with shaking hands and listened to the clock start again. He gave the adventurer Absalom's pocket watch. He says it should go on being carried by someone, and that he no longer needs it to know what time it is. He still climbs up every morning, first thing, to check that the gear is where it belongs.

### Neighbours and nuisances

Ewan cannot stand dust, and he cannot stand people touching things that swing, which is why Garrick the climber is the bane of his life. Garrick has climbed the outside of the clock tower more often than Ewan would like, which is to say more than never, and once waved to him through the face of the clock. Ewan has written to Tobin about it four times.

He knows that one of the rungs on the inside ladder was cracked last spring and mended badly. He does not know who did it. He has noticed that young Archie, the carpenter's apprentice, goes very pale whenever the ladder is mentioned, and he has his suspicions, but he would rather the boy came and told him.

His good friend Alfie, who leads the carpenters and keeps the tower stairs in repair, has told Ewan one secret: while mending an old beam in the great treehouse, Alfie found a carving that nobody can explain. Ewan has been to see it. He has told no one, not even Tobin, and he goes back now and then to look at it, the way he would listen to a clock that was ticking slightly wrong.

### What he wants and fears

Ewan wants the clock to run and the tower to stay clean. He fears that it will stop again, and that next time the gear will not come home. He also fears, though he has said it only to the clock, that whoever keeps the tower after him will not know how to listen.

### Hooks

A quest might begin when Ewan, listening one morning, hears the clock running a fraction fast, every day a little faster, as though something under the Park is pulling at it. Or he might at last ask a trusted traveller to help him understand Alfie's carving, if they can promise to keep a secret.
